meaning: 'The intoxicating one' (Old Irish medb, cognate with 'mead'), Queen of Connacht who drives the cattle raid of the Táin Bó Cúailnge.

phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) m [mʲ] — the m of 'muse', not 'mud'; Old Irish keeps the slender quality before the front vowel.
Short front [e], the stressed vowel of the name's single syllable — the 'e' of 'bed', held brief.
Lenited d, the voiced dental fricative [ð] — the soft 'th' of English 'this'; Old Irish orthography writes lenition in this position without marking it.
Final lenited b, [v] — the ancestor of the -bh of Modern Irish Meadhbh and of the English form 'Maeve'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MYETHV' — one short syllable: slender m, brief e, the d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this', finishing on 'v'. The modern Irish Meadhbh, anglicized Maeve, has collapsed the middle consonant and sounds simply 'mayv'.

kin.label: Old Irish
kin.form: Medb (genitive Medba), 'the intoxicating one'; the same word serves as the common noun medb, 'mead'

kin.label: Modern Irish
kin.form: Meadhbh, the unbroken living form — Anglicized as Maeve

kin.label: Celtic kin
kin.form: Welsh meddw, 'drunk, intoxicated' — the same adjective, worn smooth

kin.label: Indo-European root
kin.form: PIE *médhu, 'sweet drink' — English mead, Greek méthu ('wine'), and Sanskrit mádu, all one word

pronunciation.note: Medb is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Irish writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital; the queen's standing in the tradition is beside the point. The etymology, by contrast, is one of the most secure in the Celtic corpus: Old Irish medb, 'intoxicating, she who intoxicates', cognate with the noun medb, 'mead', continuing Proto-Indo-European *médhu, 'sweet drink'. The name is the sovereignty drink made personal.

domains.title: The Queen Who Chooses
domains.subtitle: The Pillow-Talk, the Bride-Gift Speech, and the Cattle Raid of Cooley
domains.lead: Medb of Crúachan is the ruling queen of Connacht and the driving will of the Táin Bó Cúailnge: the woman who audited fortunes with her husband in the night and invaded Ulster in the morning, who set the terms of her own marriages — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — and whom scholarship reads as Ireland's clearest survival of the sovereignty goddess, the land's own power to make and unmake kings.

cards.name: The Pillow-Talk
cards.desc: The night audit at Crúachan: Medb and Ailill count their wealth and find themselves equal in everything — save one bull.

cards.name: The Two Bulls
cards.desc: Finnbennach the White-Horned, who scorned a woman's keeping, and the Donn of Cúailnge — the balance of power on four legs.

cards.name: The Bride-Gift Terms
cards.desc: A husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — the bride-gift no woman before her had asked of a man of Ireland.

cards.name: Crúachan and Oweynagat
cards.desc: Her royal rath at Rathcroghan, and beneath it the Cave of the Cats — the gate of the Otherworld in the medieval tales.

symbols.name: The marriage-bed of Crúachan
symbols.meaning: The pillow-talk itself: sovereignty as an audit — equality counted coin for coin in the dark

symbols.name: The two bulls
symbols.meaning: Finnbennach and the Donn of Cúailnge: wealth, prestige, and the one point on which two rulers cannot be equal

symbols.name: The bride-gift terms
symbols.meaning: No meanness, no jealousy, no fear: the queen's own charter, demanded where a dowry was expected

symbols.name: The march of the four provinces
symbols.meaning: The raid she willed into being: armies moved by a single insistence that the account be balanced

symbols.name: Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld gate beneath her rath — the source in the tales of the things that come up on Samain night

mythology.lead: Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which.

myths.title: The Pillow-Talk
myths.text:
One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht.

That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war.

myths.title: The Bride-Gift Speech
myths.text:
The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight.

Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan.

myths.title: The Debility and the Boy at the Ford
myths.text:
Medb timed the raid for the cess noínden, the pangs of the Ulstermen — the debility laid on the warriors of Ulster by [[macha|Macha]], whom they had forced to race the king's horses when she was great with child. With Ulster's fighting-men abed, Medb marched the hosting of four provinces north — Connacht's own, the Leinster Galeóin, and the exiles of Ulster under Fergus mac Róich, who knew every road and ford of the way and, the tale says plainly, shared the queen's bed with Ailill's leave, for the road could not be found without him.

One boy stood against the whole hosting: [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], untouched by the debility, who held the fords in single combat and took the heads of the best of Connacht one by one. Medb spent everything on him — terms, ambushes, satirists, her daughter Findabair promised to a dozen champions at once — and the hardest price fell on Ferdia, Cú Chulainn's own foster-brother, whom she plied with drink and the promise of Findabair until he took the ford. Four days they fought; the gae bolga ended it; and the march went on over the body of the one man Medb could not buy twice.

myths.title: The Battle of the Bulls
myths.text:
The hosts met at Gáirech and Irgáirech when the pangs lifted and Ulster rose; Medb's army broke, but the prize was already driven south — she had the Donn of Cúailnge, and she covered the retreat herself, in the tale's most unsparing passage, when her gush of blood came on her and she asked Cú Chulainn's protection for her army's rear. He granted it: 'no coward's weapon is the weapon of a woman.' Fergus mac Róich, looking back over the ruin of the hosting, gave the raid its verdict: 'This is what usually happens to a herd of horses led by a mare — their substance is taken and carried off and destroyed as they follow a woman who has misled them.'

The bulls settled the account themselves. Finnbennach saw the Donn and bellowed; they fought through the night across Ireland, and in the morning the men of Connacht found the Brown Bull standing over the White-Horned trampled to pieces. The Donn carried Finnbennach's carcass on his horns through Connacht — scattering the loin at Áth Luain, the liver at Trim — then turned north for Cúailnge and died there of his wounds and his victory. Medb had her bull, and her equality, and the Táin's dry arithmetic: the two most valuable beasts in Ireland, both dead, and nothing left to count.

myths.title: The Cheese of Inis Cloithrinn
myths.text:
Medb outlived the raid, outlived Ailill — slain at Conall Cernach's hand — and kept her sovereignty into age, spending her last years at Inis Cloithrinn, her island on Lough Ree, where she bathed in the pool every morning at sunrise. She had killed her sister Clothru, and Clothru's son Furbaide had been cut from his mother's womb — whence his name, Ferbend, 'of the cutting' — and he grew up with the debt of it.

Furbaide found the queen's bathing place and measured it the patient way: morning after morning he stood on the shore opposite and practiced his cast against the distance, until the stone flew true by habit. Then one sunrise, as Medb came to her bath, his sling let fly — a ball of hard cheese, the tale insists, the humblest weapon in Ireland — and the queen of Connacht, who had moved four provinces against Ulster and asked no man's leave for anything in her life, died by her nephew's hand at the water's edge. Her grave, the local tradition says, is the great cairn on Knocknarea in Sligo, where she stands buried upright, facing Ulster.

lore.syncretism: The Welsh corpus preserves no Medb — but it preserves her word: Welsh meddw, 'drunk', is the same adjective, and the Mabinogi gives the Brythonic side of the theme she embodies: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] arriving as a mounted marvel no rider can catch, and the footholder Goewin whose office is bound to Math's life, are the Welsh faces of the kingship-and-goddess complex that Mac Cana traced through Irish literature. Medb's deepest kin are lexical and ritual at once. Her name is the same word as the drink by which kings were made: the Irish inauguration knew the banais ríghe, the 'wedding-feast of kingship', in which the goddess of the territory offered the king the cup — or the bed — and scholars since Mac Cana's foundational study of king and goddess have read Medb of Crúachan as that figure euhemerized into a queen. The tradition kept a second Medb to prove the point: Medb Lethderg of Tara, of whom the Book of Leinster records that she slept with nine kings of Ireland and that no king ruled at Tara who had not slept with her. Her closest kin inside the lexicon are the pantheon's other keepers of the land's consent: [[macha|Macha]], whose curse opened Ulster to her army, and [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]], who rides the same war-paths from the Otherworld side.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Táin's modern reception made Medb the most argued-over woman in Irish literature. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) carried the epic into English; Thomas Kinsella's translation (1969), with Louis le Brocquy's ink drawings, fixed the Táin as the Irish national epic for the modern reader — and Medb at its centre as its engine, not its ornament. Scholarship split over her nature: Mac Cana read her as the sovereignty goddess of Connacht demoted to a queen, the standing type-case of the king-and-goddess theme; more skeptical voices, notably J. P. Mallory's, have tested the Táin against the Iron Age record and found a tale shaped by its medieval tellers rather than a window on the pagan past. Popular culture settled the argument in its own way: the Anglicized Maeve has become one of the most fashionable Irish girls' names in the English-speaking world, and 'Queen Maeve' — the woman who wrote her own terms, chose her own husbands, and out-argued every man in the tale — stands as a feminist icon far beyond the universities. The cairn on Knocknarea that folklore calls her grave draws climbers every summer; the visitor centre at Rathcroghan interprets her rath; and in Irish itself Meadhbh never left: the living name has meant the same ungovernable queen for twelve hundred years of the written language.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Medb is the only great figure in the Celtic corpus who insists, in her own voice, on being counted equal — and then proves the point by going to war over the one item on which she was not. Read her as a goddess and she is sovereignty itself, the land auditing its king; read her as a woman and she is something rarer in medieval literature: a ruler whose motives are entirely legible and entirely her own. The pillow-talk is not vanity. It is the whole doctrine of her queenship in one scene — that the account must balance, that consent is owed to her and not by her, that a husband is a choice with terms attached.

The tradition punishes her and cannot dismiss her. The raid ends in ruin, the bulls destroy each other, the covering of the retreat is hers to do in the tale's most humiliating passage — and afterward she goes home and keeps the throne, keeps her terms, keeps choosing, until a nephew's measured patience and a piece of cheese end her at her morning bath. Medb asks the question the audit poses: what would you move an army to keep equal — and what, when the counting is done, was ever actually at stake?
lore.originalScriptNote: Old Irish writes the name Medb (genitive Medba) in the Insular Latin script of the great codices — Lebor na hUidre and the Book of Leinster preserve the Táin; normalized Old Irish spells it with plain Latin letters and no diacritic. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, carries the name-type exactly once, and in the most suggestive place in Ireland: on a stone in the Oweynagat cave at Rathcroghan, Medb's own royal complex, reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI — '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb'. Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: medb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Medb's mythic address is the best-documented royal landscape in Ireland: Crúachan Aí, the Rathcroghan complex in County Roscommon, a five-kilometre spread of more than two hundred and forty recorded monuments — ring-barrows, mounds, and enclosures — dominated by the great flat-topped Rathcroghan Mound itself. Beneath the complex opens Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats, the souterrain-fed natural cave the medieval tales call a gate of the Otherworld; within it stand two ogham stones, one reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI, '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb' — the name-type's only epigraphic attestation, at the site the tradition assigns to the queen herself. Her death-place, Inis Cloithrinn (Inchcleraun), survives as the largest island of Lough Ree on the Shannon, crowned by the early monastic ruins of Templemurray; her reputed grave is the great unexcavated Neolithic cairn (c. 3200 BCE) on the summit of Knocknarea above Sligo — Miosgán Meadhbha, 'Medb's heap', which local tradition insists she fills standing upright, spear in hand, facing Ulster. The textual witnesses are exact: the oldest substantially complete Táin (Recension I) is in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow, written at Clonmacnoise around 1106, and the fullest recension in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; O'Rahilly's editions are the modern bases. J. P. Mallory's In Search of the Irish Dreamtime (2016) is the standard archaeological cross-examination of the whole epic.
